sec.title: Objective
sec.p: The main aim of this study is to evaluate value of maternal serum nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) levels at 12 weeks in predicting the development of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) at 24–28 weeks' gestation. Other maternal variables were also evaluated, and their relationships with NRF2 levels were assessed.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted a single-center prospective cohort study including 1,270 pregnant women who attended their first-trimester antenatal visit between October 2021 and October 2023. At 12 weeks, fasting serum was collected to measure NRF2 by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and thyroid hormones on an automated chemiluminescent platform. Clinical data included age, pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, fasting plasma glucose, and lipids. All participants underwent a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at 24−28 weeks and GDM was diagnosed by International Association of the Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) criteria. Spearman correlation assessed associations between NRF2 and clinical variables. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis evaluated discrimination. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 1,270 pregnant women enrolled, 177 (13.9%) developed GDM. At 12 weeks of gestation, women who later developed GDM had significantly lower serum NRF2 levels than those without GDM. They also showed higher fasting plasma glucose (FPG), mean arterial pressure (MAP), as well as lower free thyroxine (FT4) levels. ROC analysis demonstrated that serum NRF2 at 12 weeks had good predictive value for GDM, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.779 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.745–0.812, p < 0.001). A combined model incorporating NRF2 with MAP, FT4, and FPG showed improved discrimination, with an AUC of 0.882 (95% CI 0.856−0.908, p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, lower serum NRF2 (odds ratio [OR] = 0.948, 95% CI 0.938–0.957, p < 0.001), higher MAP (OR = 1.182, 95% CI 1.132–1.233, p < 0.001), higher FPG (OR = 3.911, 95% CI 2.471−6.190, p < 0.001), and lower FT4 (OR = 0.639, 95% CI 0.562–0.726, p < 0.001) were identified as independent predictors of GDM, whereas other baseline parameters were not significant.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Decreased maternal serum NFR2 levels at 12 weeks’ gestation appear to be associated with an increased risk of developing GDM later in pregnancy. Combining this marker, together with FT4, MAP and potentially FPG may serve as a useful first-trimester screening for the risk to develop GDM.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy and is associated with substantial short- and long-term risks for mother and child [1, 2]. Recent global estimates suggest a standardized prevalence around 14%, with considerable regional variation. Pooled data from mainland China indicate rates near 15% under International Association of the Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) and World Health Organization (WHO) criteria [3–5]. GDM increases the risk of hypertensive disorders, cesarean delivery, neonatal complications, and later maternal type 2 diabetes [6, 7]. Established risk factors include higher maternal age, greater pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), prior GDM or macrosomia, and family history of diabetes; however, prevalence and effect sizes differ by population and diagnostic strategy [8, 9]. Recent studies also suggest that maternal thyroid hormone status in early pregnancy may be associated with subsequent risk of GDM [10, 11].

Early-pregnancy serum biomarkers offer objective, minimally invasive, and scalable measurements that can be integrated into routine antenatal blood draws to enable risk stratification before 24 weeks, and multi-analyte panels/algorithms consistently show incremental predictive value beyond clinical factors in external reviews and machine learning (ML)/modeling work [12–15]. Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) is reasonable mechanistic candidate. It acts as a master regulator of cellular antioxidant defenses and β-cell resilience [16]. Experimental studies have shown that NRF2 supports β-cell mass and function, and its activity is perturbed in diabetic milieus, including GDM-related tissues [17, 18]. Recent pregnancy models demonstrate that dysregulated NRF2 signaling impairs β-cell adaptation during gestation, strengthening the biological rationale for evaluating NRF2-based biomarkers [19]. Notably, despite this mechanistic foundation, clinical studies assessing maternal serum NRF2 in early pregnancy as a predictor of subsequent GDM remain scarce, with only one study reporting decreased NRF2 levels in the maternal serum of women with GDM [20].

Against this background, the present study aims to evaluate maternal serum NRF2 levels measured at 12 gestational weeks’ gestation as a biomarker for development of GDM diagnosed at 24–28 weeks. Additional maternal variables were also evaluated and their relationship to NRF2 levels assessed.

sec.title: Subjects and study design
sec.p: We conducted a single-center prospective cohort study enrolling 1,270 consecutive pregnant women attending their first-trimester antenatal visit (gestational age 10–12 weeks) between October 2021 and October 2023. Eligible participants completed a uniform baseline assessment and fasting venous blood draw at enrollment, and were scheduled for a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at 24–28 weeks’ gestation. According to the OGTT results, participants were classified into the GDM group or the non-GDM group. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) singleton intrauterine pregnancy confirmed by ultrasound; (3) gestational age at enrollment 10–12 weeks; (4) willingness and ability to complete scheduled follow-up including a 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks; and (5) provision of written informed consent. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) pregestational diabetes mellitus (type 1 or type 2) diagnosed before pregnancy or at enrollment; (2) current long-term use of medications that substantially affect glucose metabolism, including systemic glucocorticoids or other agents with significant metabolic effects; (3) preexisting major maternal disorders that could confound glucose metabolism or compromise safety, including chronic hypertension, clinically significant cardiovascular disease, severe hepatic insufficiency, or chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate < 60 mL·min⁻1·1.73 m⁻2); (4) severe obstetric complications present at or before enrollment, determined by the attending obstetrician to require inpatient management or likely to hinder participation, including persistent first-trimester vaginal bleeding with hemodynamic instability or hyperemesis gravidarum requiring parenteral therapy; (5) women subsequently identified during follow-up testing as having overt diabetes according to standard diagnostic thresholds; and (6) inability to complete scheduled follow-up or missing key baseline data. The study protocol was approved by the ethics committee of our hospital, and all participants provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Diagnosis of GDM
sec.p: At 24–28 weeks’ gestation, all participants underwent a standard 75-g, 2-h OGTT after an overnight fast of 8–12 h. Venous plasma glucose was measured at fasting, 1 h, and 2 h. GDM was diagnosed according to the IADPSG [21] if any one of the following thresholds was met: fasting ≥ 5.1 mmol/L (92 mg/dL), 1 h ≥ 10.0 mmol/L (180 mg/dL), or 2 h ≥ 8.5 mmol/L (153 mg/dL).

sec.title: Serum NRF2 levels and thyroid function assessment
sec.p: At 12 gestational weeks, fasting venous blood was collected after an overnight fast of 8–12 h into serum separator tubes; after clotting and centrifugation, serum was aliquoted and stored at − 80 °C until analysis. Serum NRF2 was quantified using a commercial sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (MBS024775, MyBioSource, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and reported as pg/mL. Thyroid function was measured on the Cobas e601 chemiluminescent immunoassay analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland) for thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH, mIU/L), free thyroxine (FT4, pmol/L), and free triiodothyronine (FT3, pmol/L), using corresponding Roche reagents. The presence of thyroid autoimmune antibodies was assessed using the Elecsys Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb) (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland; catalog No. 06368590 190 V4.0) with a measuring range of 5.00–600 IU/mL, and TPOAb positivity defined as ≥ 34 IU/mL according to the manufacturer’s reference interval. All assays were performed in the central laboratory by personnel blinded to clinical outcomes.

sec.title: Clinical data collection
sec.p: Baseline and follow-up data were obtained with a standardized case report form at 12 gestational weeks and again at the 24–28-week OGTT visit. Collected variables included (1) maternal age; (2) height and pre-pregnancy weight to calculate BMI; (3) parity status (primiparous vs multiparous); (4) family history of diabetes in first-degree relatives; (5) systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) measured with an automated upper-arm oscillometric device after ≥ 5 min of seated rest (HEM-907, Omron Healthcare, Kyoto, Japan), and mean arterial pressure (MAP) was subsequently calculated as DBP plus one-third of the pulse pressure, that is, DBP + 1/3(SBP-DBP); (6) fasting plasma glucose (FPG), total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) assayed in fasting serum on a fully automated clinical chemistry analyzer (Cobas c702, Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland) using the hexokinase method for glucose and enzymatic colorimetric assays for lipids; (7) a 75-g OGTT performed at 24–28 gestational weeks after 8–12 h of fasting, with venous plasma glucose measured at 0, 1, and 2 h on the same analyzer under standard operating procedures. Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) was measured at the OGTT visit (24–28 gestational weeks) according to standard laboratory procedures.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software (version 26.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were tested for normality using Shapiro–Wilk test. Normally distributed data are presented as mean ± SD and compared with the independent samples t test, while non-normally distributed data are expressed as median (IQR) and compared with Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables are summarized as n (%) and compared using the χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test as appropriate. Correlations between serum NRF2 and thyroid function indices were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. The predictive performance of candidate indicators for GDM was evaluated by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, with calculation of the area under the curve (AUC) and the optimal cutoff determined by Youden’s index. Multivariate binary logistic regression analysis was conducted to identify independent predictors of GDM. Results are expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A two-tailed P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Baseline clinical characteristics of participants
sec.p:
A total of 1,270 pregnant women were enrolled in the study, of whom 177 (13.9%) were diagnosed with GDM based on the 24–28-week OGTT results, and 1,093 (86.1%) were classified as non-GDM. Compared with the non-GDM group, women with GDM had significantly higher MAP (Table 1, p < 0.05), as well as higher FPG, higher HbA1c levels, and elevated glucose levels at all OGTT time points (0 h, 1 h, and 2 h, all p < 0.05). However, there were no significant differences between the two groups in maternal age, pre-pregnancy BMI, lipid profile (TC, TG, HDL-C, LDL-C), parity status, family history of diabetes, or TPOAb positivity (p > 0.05).Table 1

sec.title: Serum NRF2 and early thyroid indices in all participants
sec.p:
At 12 weeks of gestation, women who subsequently developed GDM showed significantly lower serum NRF2 levels compared with the non-GDM group (p < 0.05, Fig. 1). Serum TSH levels did not differ significantly between the two groups (p = 0.322). Serum FT4 levels were significantly lower in the GDM group (p < 0.05), while serum FT3 levels were significantly higher (p = 0.023). The FT3/FT4 ratio was also significantly higher in women with GDM compared with those without GDM (p < 0.05, Fig. 1).Fig. 1
Serum nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and thyroid function indices measured at 12 weeks of gestation in all subjects

sec.title: Association between serum NRF2 and clinical variables
sec.p:
Spearman’s correlation analysis was conducted to assess the relationships between serum NRF2 levels and clinical characteristics at 12 weeks of gestation (Table 2). Serum NRF2 levels were weakly negatively correlated with fasting plasma glucose (r = − 0.056, p = 0.045) and with the FT3/FT4 ratio (r = − 0.064, p = 0.023). No significant correlations were found between NRF2 and maternal age, BMI, MAP, lipid profile (TG, HDL-C, LDL-C), HbA1c levels, or other thyroid function indices (TSH, FT4, FT3) (p > 0.05) (Fig. 2).Table 2

sec.title: Predictive value of early-pregnancy serum NRF2 for GDM
sec.p:
ROC analysis was performed using serum NRF2 levels measured at 12 gestational weeks to identify women who later developed GDM at 24–28 weeks. The AUC was 0.779 (95% CI 0.745–0.812, p < 0.001). The optimal cutoff value determined by the Youden’s index was 163.99 pg/mL, yielding a sensitivity of 70.0% and a specificity of 66.7%. To further improve predictive performance, a combined model incorporating serum NRF2, MAP, FPG, and FT4 was constructed. The combined ROC analysis demonstrated a significantly improved AUC of 0.882 (95% CI 0.856–0.908, p < 0.001), with a sensitivity of 79.1% and a specificity of 79.7%. To facilitate clinical interpretability, we further reported sensitivities at prespecified false positive rates. At false positive rates of 10%, 15%, and 20% (corresponding to specificities of 90%, 85%, and 80%), the sensitivities of the combined model were 62.7%, 72.9%, and 78.0%, respectively (Fig. 3).Fig. 3

sec.title: Multivariable logistic regression: early predictors of GDM
sec.p:
In the multivariable binary logistic regression, serum NRF2 remained an independent predictor of GDM (OR = 0.948, 95% CI 0.938–0.957, p < 0.001; Table 3). Among other covariates, higher MAP (OR = 1.182, 95% CI 1.132–1.233, p < 0.001), higher FPG (OR = 3.911, 95% CI 2.471–6.190, p < 0.001), and lower FT4 (OR = 0.639, 95% CI 0.562–0.726, p < 0.001) were independently associated with GDM. Maternal age, pre-pregnancy BMI, TC, TG, HDL-C, LDL-C, TSH, FT3, parity, and TPOAb positivity were not significantly associated with GDM after adjustment (all p > 0.05; Table 3).Table 3

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Early identification of women at risk for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is crucial because GDM is linked to hypertensive disorders, cesarean delivery, neonatal complications, and elevated long-term risks of type 2 diabetes in mothers and dysglycemia in offspring [22]. In routine care, diagnosis is typically established with a 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks, which limits opportunities for prevention earlier in pregnancy; evidence for screening and treating before 24 weeks remains mixed, underscoring the need for reliable early-pregnancy predictors [23]. In our study, measured at 12 gestational weeks, women who later developed GDM showed lower serum NRF2. In addition, ROC analysis demonstrated that early-pregnancy NRF2 had significant discriminative value for predicting GDM.

In our cohort with baseline at 12 weeks, women who developed GDM showed a lower FT4 and a higher FT3/FT4 ratio, while TSH and TPOAb positivity did not differ from the non-GDM group. Wang et al. reported that a lower early-pregnancy FT4 and a higher FT3/FT4 ratio were associated with subsequent GDM, which is consistent with our results [11]. Yang et al. also observed that reduced FT4 in early pregnancy was linked with increased GDM risk, supporting the direction of effect we found [10]. Regarding the FT3/FT4 ratio, Raets et al. identified higher ratios as related to GDM in the Belgian Diabetes in Pregnancy study cohort, and Zhao et al. reported positive correlations between first-trimester FT3/FT4 and glucose levels, both aligning with our data [24, 25]. For TSH, several analyses describe mixed or null associations once FT4 and covariates are accounted for, which mirrors our observation of no between-group difference [26]. Moreover, our null finding for TPOAb is compatible with heterogeneous literature: an earlier meta-analysis suggested only a small increase in GDM risk with TPOAb positivity, while subsequent studies have yielded inconsistent associations [27].

Our data place early-pregnancy serum NRF2 within a growing body of biomarker research for GDM. In a large Shanghai cohort, higher uric acid at 13–18 weeks showed a nonlinear association with later GDM, with risk increasing across quintiles and more pronounced among women aged ≥ 35 years [28]. In contrast, a Foshan cohort reported no association between first-trimester 25-hydroxy vitamin D and GDM despite multiple correlations with other routine laboratory parameters [29]. First-trimester NGAL was higher in women who subsequently developed GDM and showed good discriminatory performance in prediction models, supporting its potential utility as an early marker [30]. A meta-analysis on afamin found higher first-trimester levels among pregnancies that later developed GDM, while results in later gestation were inconsistent, indicating gestational timing may matter for performance [31]. Taken together, these studies highlight heterogeneous but complementary biomarker signals across oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolic pathways. Our finding that lower serum NRF2 at 12 weeks is linked to incident GDM adds a redox-regulatory dimension that may be valuable when integrated with routine clinical factors and other circulating markers.

We observed that maternal serum NRF2 at 12 weeks was lower in women who later developed GDM. We interpret this finding in the context of mechanistic studies showing that NRF2 supports β-cell adaptation and helps maintain placental redox balance during pregnancy. In a β-cell-specific knockout model, loss of NRF2reduced β-cell proliferation, increased oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, impaired insulin secretory function, and limited the gestational expansion of β-cell mass. Estrogen upregulated NRF2 in β-cells and protected against oxidative stress through this pathway, highlighting NRF2 as a key node in the physiology of late gestation and a potential therapeutic target for GDM [19]. A placental study demonstrated that suppression of NRF2 and its downstream target heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) under high-glucose conditions contributed to oxidative stress and impaired trophoblast function in GDM [32]. Preclinical GDM models also indicate that restoring NRF2 signaling improves redox homeostasis and metabolic disturbance. Activation of NRF2–HO-1 corrected GDM-related increases in reactive oxygen species, apoptosis, and inflammatory mediators, and it ameliorated hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia in vivo and in vitro [33]. Taken together, these lines of evidence position NRF2 as a central regulator at the interface of β-cell adaptation and placental oxidative stress. In our study, we found that lower maternal serum NRF2 at 12 weeks was associated with subsequent GDM and independently predicted GDM risk on multivariable analysis.

From a clinical perspective, the present findings support the concept of early risk stratification rather than the use of serum NRF2 as a single standalone screening marker. Early risk assessment may integrate maternal serum NRF2 levels at 12 gestational weeks with routine clinical measures, such as blood pressure and thyroid function indices, to improve risk stratification. Women identified as being at higher risk could benefit from closer monitoring and early, non-pharmacological interventions, including counseling on diet, physical activity, and gestational weight gain targets, as well as earlier referral to nutrition services. Enhanced surveillance strategies may include home blood pressure monitoring and short-term capillary glucose profiling, with the 75-g oral glucose tolerance test scheduled at the earliest appropriate window within 24–28 weeks of gestation. Importantly, NRF2 should be regarded as a risk marker rather than a diagnostic test, and any escalation of care should aim to prevent or delay hyperglycemia while preserving the oral glucose tolerance test as the diagnostic standard. These proposed approaches illustrate potential clinical implications of early risk identification and require validation in future prospective interventional studies.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This single-center prospective cohort limits generalizability to other regions and care settings. The observational design precludes causal inference despite multivariable adjustment. Serum NRF2 and thyroid indices were measured once at 12 weeks, so biological variability and temporal trajectories were not captured. Assays were performed with one analytical platform, and cross-platform harmonization was not evaluated. This study was powered for group comparisons and primary prediction analysis, yet subgroup effects and rare exposures may be underpowered. The discriminative performance of NRF2 was modest and requires external validation and clinical utility assessment before implementation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, this paper provides a multiple markers approach for 12 weeks screening of the risk to develop GDM using NRF2 combined with MAP, FT4, and FPG. In this way, the screening efficacy generates an area under the multiple marker ROC curve of 0.882 and a detection rate of 62.7% at a 10% false positive rate, providing a promising clinical tool for early prediction of the risk to develop GDM. Further studies with external validation are warranted.
